Highly classified US national security communications network goes down

Highly classified US national security communications network goes down

AI 作者 monkeydust 热度 639 回复 715 2026/11/17 23:38
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter.
  • The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue.

lancebeet 2026/11/18 21:58
Since agents got really at this, I've used them to uncover quite a few verifiable vulnerabilities. Some were easily patchable oversights, but others uncovered flawed architectural decisions which required significant rewrites to fix (done with agents, of course), with a non-zero probability of regressions. I guess your assumption here depends on your definitions of "knowing how to code" and "leveraging AI properly" but it's definitely possible for someone with years of professional experience as a software developer, using the best AI tools on the market, to unintentionally break something when they fix something else.

These are huge systems with multiple application, data, and network layers. usernomdeguerre 2026/11/18 03:11
People seem to be leaning on the AI speculation from the "vibe coded" angle, but couldn't this also be an "AI is the reason" from the attacker side? I think we've seen more than a fair share of AI assisted exploits that chain many small vulnerabilities into something more pronounced. I'm thinking of the rash of attacks in SK and China against Banks using offensive harnesses.

I'd be more willing to believe the network in question here was under an attack load that either was probed or exploited far enough that shutting it down was worthwhile. It seems more reasonable to me than believing they've let AI run amok on their internals such that it's now failing.

Not because I'm deifying the NSA but because the system has to be decades old, at least, and I wouldn't expect significant changes to something that "just works".
